subtopic_detail: Body focused repetitive behaviour and the treatment that comes before medication
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19 year old university student who has been wearing a beanie indoors for three months. She tells you she pulls hair from her scalp while studying and watching television, sometimes without noticing she has started.

She describes a build up of tension beforehand and a sense of relief afterwards, and she has tried repeatedly to stop. She does not eat the hair. She denies any belief that her hair is abnormal or that she looks disfigured, and she is not checking mirrors or seeking cosmetic procedures. On examination there is an irregular patch of hair loss over the right parietal scalp containing hairs of varying lengths, with normal skin, no scaling, no scarring and no broken exclamation mark hairs.

data_table.Examination: Irregular right parietal patch of hair loss with hairs of differing lengths, normal underlying scalp skin, no scaling or scarring, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily and review her response after six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants are effective for obsessive compulsive disorder but have performed poorly for hair pulling in trials, and they are not the first choice here (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Refer to dermatology for a scalp biopsy to clarify the pattern of loss
options.rationale: Biopsy would be needed if scarring alopecia or alopecia areata were plausible, and hairs of differing lengths in an irregular patch with normal skin already give the diagnosis (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

options.text: Start low dose olanzapine at night and monitor her weight monthly
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation has limited trial support in this condition and carries metabolic cost that is hard to justify before behavioural treatment has been tried (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reassure her that the habit is common and review her again in six months
options.rationale: Repeated failed attempts to stop plus visible hair loss and social avoidance define a disorder rather than a habit, and passive review offers her nothing (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training with a trained psychologist
options.rationale: Habit reversal training, which combines awareness training, a competing response and stimulus control, has the strongest evidence base of any treatment for hair pulling and is the recommended first step (Source: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

explanation.summary: Hair pulling disorder sits in the obsessive compulsive and related group but responds differently to treatment from obsessive compulsive disorder itself, which is the main clinical trap. Behavioural treatment outperforms medication, and awareness training matters because much of the pulling is automatic rather than deliberate. Two questions separate it from its neighbours: whether the person believes something is wrong with their appearance, which would suggest body dysmorphic disorder, and whether the hair is swallowed, which raises trichobezoar and warrants abdominal assessment. Dermatological mimics are excluded at the bedside by looking for scarring, scaling and exclamation mark hairs rather than by biopsy.
key_points: Hairs of varying length in an irregular patch with normal skin indicates pulling
Habit reversal training is the first line treatment
Serotonergic antidepressants perform less well here than in obsessive compulsive disorder
Ask about swallowing hair because of the risk of trichobezoar
Appearance related beliefs would point instead to body dysmorphic disorder
explanation.pearls: Ask every patient who pulls hair whether they swallow it, because trichophagia can produce a gastric trichobezoar with the tail extending into the small bowel and presenting years later as obstruction.

sources.label: RANZCP Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: Persisting bereavement reaction beyond the diagnostic time threshold
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old woman 15 months after her husband died of pancreatic cancer. She tells you she thinks about him for most of the day, longs for him constantly, and still cannot bring herself to enter the room where he died or to give away his clothes.

She says she feels that part of her died with him and that she no longer knows who she is without him. She has stopped seeing the friends they had as a couple. She sleeps and eats reasonably and has not lost weight. She has no pervasive anhedonia, no feelings of worthlessness unrelated to the loss, and no suicidal ideation, although she says she would not mind if she did not wake up. She is still doing her job but has taken no interest in it.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband, reactive affect at other times, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, no plan or intent to harm herself
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her that this is normal grief and offer review in six months
options.rationale: Intense yearning with identity disruption and avoidance that persists past 12 months with functional impairment has crossed from expected grief into a diagnosable disorder (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night to address her sleep and appetite as well
options.rationale: An antidepressant would be the choice if she met criteria for a depressive episode, and her sleep, appetite and weight are preserved with no pervasive anhedonia (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

options.text: Refer for structured grief focused psychotherapy with a psychologist
options.rationale: Targeted grief focused psychotherapy, which pairs exposure to avoided reminders with work on restoring life goals, outperforms both antidepressants and general supportive counselling for this presentation (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders; DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Prescribe short term temazepam to help her sleep and review in a month
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not improve grief outcomes, risk dependence, and blunt the emotional processing that treatment depends on (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer her to a community bereavement support group run by volunteers
options.rationale: Peer support helps uncomplicated bereavement, but it has not been shown to resolve the avoidance and identity disruption that define the disorder (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders).

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder was added as a formal diagnosis to recognise a minority of bereaved people, around one in twenty, whose grief remains intense and disabling rather than gradually integrating. The threshold in adults is at least 12 months from the death, with persistent yearning or preoccupation plus features such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness and a sense that life is meaningless. It overlaps with but is distinct from major depression, where guilt, worthlessness and anhedonia are pervasive rather than focused on the deceased, and from post traumatic stress disorder. Getting the distinction right matters because the first line treatment is a specific psychotherapy rather than an antidepressant.
key_points: The adult time threshold is 12 months from the death
Yearning and preoccupation with the deceased are the core symptoms
Depression brings pervasive anhedonia and worthlessness beyond the loss
Grief focused psychotherapy is the first line treatment
Antidepressants are added when a comorbid depressive episode is present
explanation.pearls: Avoidance of reminders is the feature that most reliably distinguishes prolonged grief from ordinary bereavement, and it is also the specific target of the exposure component of grief focused therapy.

subtopic_detail: Somatic complaints confined to school mornings in early adolescence
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 12 year old boy brought by his mother because he has missed 14 of the last 20 school days with stomach aches and nausea. The symptoms begin as he is getting dressed and are severe enough that he cries and refuses to get in the car.

Once the decision is made that he can stay home he settles within an hour, and he is entirely well at weekends and through the recent school holidays. His mother has been working from home so that she can stay with him. He tells you he worries that something bad will happen to his mother while he is at school and that he cannot concentrate for thinking about it. He denies being bullied and his teachers report he is academically capable. His growth is normal and his abdomen is soft and non tender.

data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen, no organomegaly, growth tracking along the 50th centile, normal general examination
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C-reactive protein, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a graded return to school with the school and family together
options.rationale: Early graded return coordinated between clinician, family and school, with anxiety management skills alongside it, is the intervention with the best outcomes and it works better the sooner attendance resumes (Source: RANZCP Child and Adolescent Psychiatry; RCH CPG: School Refusal).

options.text: Start sertraline 25 mg daily and review his symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication is added when psychological treatment has not succeeded or when a severe comorbid disorder is present, not as the opening move in a treatable anxiety presentation (Source: RANZCP Child and Adolescent Psychiatry).

options.text: Refer to gastroenterology for endoscopy to investigate the abdominal pain
options.rationale: Symptoms confined to school mornings with normal growth, examination and screening tests do not fit organic disease, and further investigation reinforces the illness belief (Source: RCH CPG: School Refusal).

options.text: Support a period of home schooling until his anxiety symptoms settle
options.rationale: Withdrawal from school relieves the anxiety in the short term and reinforces avoidance, and the longer the absence the harder the eventual return (Source: RCH CPG: School Refusal).

options.text: Notify the education department of unauthorised absence from school
options.rationale: An enforcement response fits truancy, in which the young person conceals the absence and spends the day elsewhere, and this boy stays home with his parents' knowledge and is distressed (Source: RCH CPG: School Refusal).

explanation.summary: School refusal is anxiety driven non attendance with the parents' knowledge, and it is distinguished from truancy by the distress, the disclosure and the fact that the child stays at home. Somatic symptoms that appear on school mornings and vanish at weekends and holidays are the pattern that makes the diagnosis without extensive investigation. Separation anxiety, social anxiety, generalised anxiety and undetected learning difficulties or bullying all sit behind it and should be screened for. Prognosis worsens with the duration of absence, so the plan is measured in days rather than terms, and it must involve the school directly because a plan agreed only in the consulting room fails on the first morning.
key_points: Symptoms that disappear at weekends and holidays point away from organic disease
School refusal involves parental knowledge and distress, unlike truancy
Return to school is graded but starts early because prognosis worsens with time
The school must be part of the plan, not just the family
Screen for bullying, learning difficulty and parental mental illness
explanation.pearls: Every week of continued absence lowers the likelihood of successful return, so a partial attendance plan starting within days beats a complete plan that waits for a psychology appointment in six weeks.

subtopic_detail: Treating attention deficit hyperactivity disorder when a tic disorder coexists
stem:
You are the paediatrician reviewing a 9 year old boy who has had eye blinking and shoulder shrugging for two years, with intermittent throat clearing. The movements come and go in intensity, do not hurt him, and he says other children have stopped commenting on them.

His parents' concern today is different. He cannot stay in his seat, loses his belongings weekly, and his teacher reports he completes about a third of set work. Structured rating scales completed by parents and two teachers meet criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, combined presentation, with impairment at home and at school. His father asks you directly whether starting a stimulant will make the movements worse, because a relative told him it would.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 100/62, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Intermittent eye blinking and shoulder shrugs suppressible on request, normal neurological examination, growth on the 60th centile for height and weight
data_table.Rating scales: Parent and two teacher scales meet criteria for combined presentation with cross setting impairment; tic severity rated mild with no functional impact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the movements first with comprehensive behavioural intervention
options.rationale: Behavioural therapy for tics is the right first step when the tics are the impairing problem, and here they are mild and not troubling him while the attentional symptoms are disabling (Source: RANZCP Neurodevelopmental Disorders).

options.text: Start methylphenidate for the attentional symptoms and monitor his tics
options.rationale: Controlled data show stimulants do not worsen tics on average and treating the impairing condition is the priority, with tic severity tracked at each review so the family is not left guessing (Source: RANZCP Neurodevelopmental Disorders; Australian ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Start clonidine as a single agent to cover both sets of symptoms
options.rationale: Clonidine does treat both and is a reasonable choice when tics are moderate to severe, but its effect on the core attentional symptoms is substantially smaller than that of a stimulant (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline).

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and review his movements in six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are effective for severe tics but carry weight gain, metabolic and extrapyramidal risk that is unjustifiable for mild tics with no functional impact (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Defer all medication and reassess both problems again in six months
options.rationale: Deferral leaves a child completing a third of his schoolwork untreated for another half year, and untreated symptoms carry academic and self esteem costs (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline).

explanation.summary: Tic disorders and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder co-occur frequently, and the historical warning that stimulants provoke tics has not held up in controlled trials, where tic severity follows its natural waxing and waning course regardless of treatment. The practical approach is to identify which condition is causing the impairment and to treat that one. Mild tics that the child has adapted to need explanation and monitoring rather than drug treatment, since most tic disorders improve through adolescence. When tics are the impairing problem, comprehensive behavioural intervention is first line, with alpha 2 agonists or antipsychotics for more severe cases. Naming the myth explicitly and offering to track tic severity is what keeps the family engaged with treatment.
key_points: Stimulants do not worsen tics on average in controlled trials
Treat whichever condition is causing the functional impairment
Most tic disorders improve through adolescence
Behavioural intervention is first line when tics are impairing
Alpha 2 agonists treat both but are weaker for attentional symptoms
explanation.pearls: Tics naturally wax and wane over weeks, so an increase in the fortnight after a stimulant is started is far more likely to be the natural course than a drug effect, and stopping treatment on that basis costs the child an effective medication.

subtopic_detail: Behavioural addiction presenting as insomnia and anxiety in primary care
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 45 year old man who asks for something to help him sleep. He works as a plumber and says he lies awake with his heart racing.

On questioning he tells you he has been betting on sport through an app for three years. Over the past eight months the stakes have grown, he returns the next day to win back what he lost, and he has taken out a personal loan and a credit card that his wife does not know about. He has twice promised her he had stopped. He drinks four standard drinks a week, uses no other substances, and has no previous psychiatric history. He looks tired and says quietly that his family would be better off without him, although he has no plan and wants help.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Anxious and tired appearing, reactive affect, no psychotic features, no intoxication or withdrawal signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a short course of temazepam and review his sleep in two weeks
options.rationale: Sedative prescribing treats the presenting complaint while leaving the driver untouched, and it adds dependence risk in a man who has just expressed passive suicidal thoughts (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start sertraline for anxiety and arrange to see him again in one month
options.rationale: Antidepressants have no established role in gambling disorder itself, and a month is too long an interval given the risk he has disclosed today (Source: RANZCP Addiction Psychiatry).

options.text: Advise him to self exclude from betting apps and review him in one month
options.rationale: Self exclusion and app blocking are useful components of a plan and are undermined when offered alone, because they do not address the craving, the debt or the risk (Source: RANZCP Addiction Psychiatry).

options.text: Assess suicide risk today and refer to a gambling specific psychology service
options.rationale: Suicide risk in gambling disorder is high and the passive ideation he has disclosed requires assessment and a safety plan at this visit, alongside referral for the cognitive behavioural treatment that has the best evidence (Source: RANZCP Addiction Psychiatry).

options.text: Refer him to a financial counsellor to consolidate his debts and review later
options.rationale: Financial counselling is a valuable part of the plan, but debt restructuring without treatment of the disorder frequently funds further gambling (Source: RANZCP Addiction Psychiatry).

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is the one behavioural addiction recognised in the diagnostic manuals, and people almost never present with it as the stated problem, arriving instead with insomnia, anxiety, relationship breakdown or a physical complaint. The features to elicit are escalating stakes, chasing losses, concealment, failed attempts to stop and continued gambling despite consequences. Rates of suicidal ideation and attempts are markedly elevated compared with the general population, driven by debt and shame, so risk assessment belongs at the first consultation rather than at review. Cognitive behavioural therapy has the strongest evidence, delivered face to face or through national telephone and online services, with financial counselling, partner involvement and self exclusion as adjuncts. Naltrexone is a second line option for craving in selected patients.
key_points: People with gambling disorder rarely name it as the presenting problem
Chasing losses and concealment are core diagnostic features
Suicide risk is substantially elevated and is assessed at the first visit
Cognitive behavioural therapy has the best evidence for treatment
Self exclusion and financial counselling are adjuncts, not the whole plan
explanation.pearls: Two screening questions, whether he has ever felt he needed to bet more money and whether he has ever lied about how much he gambles, detect most cases and take under a minute in a consultation about insomnia.
